  ## How tech and trading sites teach their product, and what to copy for the herding app
  
  I edited no project files and wrote no notes.
  
  ### What each site does best
  - **Stripe** ([docs.stripe.com/testing](https://docs.stripe.com/testing)): gives you one safe, memorable value to try first ("4242 4242 4242 4242, any future date, any CVC"). It then lists scenario tables (Description | Number | Result) so you can trigger each outcome on purpose, for example "Generic decline".
  - **Brilliant**: you do a problem before you read about it, in small steps. Its homepage is now mostly about its tutor "Koji", so this note comes partly from memory.
  - **Duolingo**: lets you play before signing up, then shows a "Lesson Complete" screen with XP (points) and a progress ring. Source: third-party teardowns ([Appcues](https://goodux.appcues.com/blog/duolingo-user-onboarding), [userguiding](https://userguiding.com/blog/duolingo-onboarding-ux)), not first-hand.
  - **TradingView**: each indicator help page uses the same four parts: Definition, Calculation, What to look for, and hedged readings ("suggests", "may hint"). The RSI link I tried served the MACD page instead. Its "Ideas" help pages returned 404.
  - **Fidelity Learning Center**: one-rule cards that lead with a real number and a short label ("15% First things first", "60% must-have expenses").
  - **Linear** ([start-guide](https://linear.app/docs/start-guide), [conceptual model](https://linear.app/docs/conceptual-model)): a demo workspace to look around before your own, one concept per heading, and a closing "How these concepts fit together" recap.
  - **Figma**: prefilled "Figma Basics" example files plus an opt-in tooltip tour. Source: [supademo](https://supademo.com/content/plg-onboarding-gallery/figma) and Appcues, secondary only.
  - **PhET** ([Podolefsky, Moore & Perkins, "Implicit scaffolding"](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.6544)): the guidance is built into the simulation itself, not written out, so students are guided "without feeling guided".
  - **Khan Academy**: worked example, then practice with hints, then mastery levels. Its pages blocked me, so this is from memory.
  - **Desmos**: if you type an undefined letter, it offers a slider for it, which turns a symbol into something you can move. Its pages blocked me, so this is from memory.
  
  ### PhET's published design principles (arXiv 1306.6544, pp. 7-12)
  - **Scope:** each simulation targets a few named learning goals.
  - **Sequence:** tabs go from simple to complex. Later tabs relax earlier limits, so the help fades as students go.
  - **Opening screen:** interesting but simple to read, so nobody feels overwhelmed.
  - **First action:** one obvious action, cued by color and position rather than text, that gives immediate positive feedback.
  - **Familiar controls:** normal buttons and sliders.
  - **Low risk:** a big "Reset all" button and easy undo.
  - **Representations:** linked by placing labels close to what they name, by shared color, and by feedback that arrives at the same moment.
  - **Immediate, readable feedback:** no feedback reads as "nothing happened".
  - **Layout:** the basics sit centrally and at the top of toolboxes. Students look at the center first, then read toolboxes from top to bottom.
  - **Minimal wording:** short labels next to the objects they name.
  - **Bounded ranges:** slider limits are picked so the extremes teach something, since students try the extremes.
  - **Illuminating cases:** scene buttons that jump to the most useful comparisons.
  - **Puzzles and challenges:** built in, to keep students exploring and let them check themselves.
  - **Defaults:** readouts start off, and settings start at moderate values.

  1. **One obvious first action** (PhET). *Test program.* Open with every extra control collapsed and only the "Herding strength (a1)" slider plus a primary "Run model" button visible. Use `st.expander` for the rest, and give the start state a CSS glow through `st.html`.

Use `st.segmented_control` instead, and add a one-line "what to expect" caption per preset, Stripe-style.
  3. **Big, safe Reset** (PhET). *Test program.* A `st.button("Reset all")` that clears the `session_state` keys and calls `st.rerun()`.

def _cap(u):
    return min(U_CAP, max(-U_CAP, u))


def _simulate(g, days, steps, chartists, N, v1, v2, a1, a2, a3, s, R, tc, gamma,
              beta, sigma_mu, sigma_eps, tick, floor, n_plus, n_minus, max_gap, max_days,
              hard_gap, cb1, cb2, cb3, halt_steps, pause_end, shock):
    """The simulation loop (see SPEC.md). Returns per-day log price, log value,
    chartist share and opinion at each day's close, the circuit-breaker level of
    each day, and the number of days completed (fewer than `days` if the price ran
    away: |log price - log value| above max_gap for max_days days in a row, or ever
    above hard_gap).
    Circuit breakers: 0 > cb1 > cb2 > cb3 are log falls from the previous close
    (-inf = off). Falling to cb1 or cb2 within the first pause_end steps of the day
    freezes the price for halt_steps steps (once each per day; later in the day
    nothing happens); falling to cb3 freezes it for the rest of the day, at any time.
    Traders keep switching while the price is frozen.
    shock[day]: log change of the value at the start of that day (policy surprise).
    The last value returned says whether the run ran away (on any day, the last included;
    more than MAX_TICKS ticks in one step also counts, so no random draw is asked for
    an absurd number)."""
    dt = 1.0 / steps
    window = int(round(TREND_WINDOW * steps))
    up_step, down_step = np.log(1.0 + tick), np.log(1.0 - tick)
    # mu is drawn fresh each step; scaled so its effect per day does not depend on
    # dt (identical to [S] at their dt = 0.01)
    mu_sd = sigma_mu * np.sqrt(REFERENCE_DT / dt)
    news_sd = sigma_eps * np.sqrt(dt)          # the news of one step (sec. 4)
    lp = 0.0                                   # log price; starts at the value
    lf = 0.0                                   # log fundamental value
    n_f = N - n_plus - n_minus
    past = np.zeros(window)                    # log prices of the last `window` steps
    out_lp = np.empty(days + 1)
    out_lf = np.empty(days + 1)
    out_z = np.empty(days + 1)
    out_x = np.empty(days + 1)
    out_lp[0], out_lf[0] = lp, lf
    nc = n_plus + n_minus
    out_z[0] = nc / N
    out_x[0] = (n_plus - n_minus) / nc if nc > 0 else 0.0
    halts = np.zeros(days, dtype=np.int64)     # 0 none, 1-2 pause levels, 3 closed
    t = 0
    outside = 0                                # days in a row beyond max_gap
    for day in range(days):
        lf += shock[day]
        prev_close = lp
        paused = 0                             # steps of pause left
        for k in range(steps):
            # dp/dt / p: relative price change per day over the trend window
            trend = (np.exp(lp - past[t % window]) - 1.0) / TREND_WINDOW
            past[t % window] = lp
            t += 1
            gap = np.exp(lf - lp) - 1.0        # (p_f - p) / p
            if chartists:
                nc = n_plus + n_minus
                # sec. 1: mood. sec. 2: strategy (profit of chartists vs fundamentalists)
                U1 = _cap(a1 * (n_plus - n_minus) / nc + a2 / v1 * trend)
                gain = R * (1.0 + gap) + trend / v2    # (r + (dp/dt)/v2) / p, r = R p_f
                U21 = _cap(a3 * (gain - R - s * abs(gap)))
                U22 = _cap(a3 * (R - gain - s * abs(gap)))
                mood = v1 * nc / N
                # every rate below is per trader per day (first: where they go)
                p_to_m, p_to_f = _leave(g, n_plus, mood * np.exp(-U1),
                                        v2 * n_f / N * np.exp(-U21), dt)
                m_to_p, m_to_f = _leave(g, n_minus, mood * np.exp(U1),
                                        v2 * n_f / N * np.exp(-U22), dt)
                f_to_p, f_to_m = _leave(g, n_f, v2 * n_plus / N * np.exp(U21),
                                        v2 * n_minus / N * np.exp(U22), dt)
                # floors (sec. 5): undo just enough moves to keep both groups alive
                short_f = floor - (n_f - f_to_p - f_to_m + p_to_f + m_to_f)
                while short_f > 0:
                    if f_to_p >= f_to_m:
                        f_to_p -= 1
                    else:
                        f_to_m -= 1
                    short_f -= 1
                short_c = floor - (nc - p_to_f - m_to_f + f_to_p + f_to_m)
                while short_c > 0:
                    if p_to_f >= m_to_f:
                        p_to_f -= 1
                    else:
                        m_to_f -= 1
                    short_c -= 1
                n_plus += m_to_p - p_to_m + f_to_p - p_to_f
                n_minus += p_to_m - m_to_p + f_to_m - m_to_f
                n_f += p_to_f + m_to_f - f_to_p - f_to_m
            # sec. 3: excess demand -> random up and down ticks
            ed = (n_plus - n_minus) * tc + n_f * gamma * gap
            # ticks per day = beta (ED + mu) / tick, so that on average
            # (dp/dt)/p = beta (ED + mu), SPEC eq. 25 (the log price moves slightly
            # less: ln(1 + tick) per up-tick, not tick)

# Analysis scripts

Each script answers one question about the rebuilt model and prints the numbers
quoted in `figures/RESULTS.md` and `KEY_POINTS.md`. They use the fitted settings
in `settings/` and held-out seeds only. Run from the project folder, e.g.
`python3 scripts/analysis/long_run_stability.py`.

| Script | Question |
|---|---|
| `efficient_market_claims.py` | Lux & Marchesi's efficient-market claims: price = value on average, no persistent mispricing, volatility vs chartist share |
| `bounce_back_after_big_days.py` | After a big move, does the price bounce back (like the S&P) or keep sliding? |
| `president_terms.py` | Term by term: which presidencies can the politics-free model explain? (Fig 12b) |
| `president_party_gap.py` | Is the S&P different under Democratic and Republican presidents, beyond luck? (Fig 12) |
| `party_scale.py` | The party test at scale: 24 markets (Dow 1896–, S&P, Nasdaq, 20 stocks) against 1,000 model histories, with a bootstrap range and each presidency left out in turn |
| `news_and_reactions.py` | Do traders react logically to news? The model's moves against its own news (with and without herding), the Dow's reaction to 33 presidential elections, and the documented causes of its 20 biggest days |
| `time_step_check.py` | Do results change with the time step dt? (`spx` or `paper`; the paper-matched ones do) |
| `test_accuracy_audit.py` | How accurate is each noisy test? Bias and sd of every checked number over 200 seeds, and the tolerance \|bias\| + 5 sd the tests use (`docs/TEST_ACCURACY.md`) |
| `web_stress_test.py` | Is the web app precise, fast and correct on all the data? Every market's numbers recomputed independently (scipy, plain loops), a herding x seed grid, slider corners, live Yahoo vs saved files, every page run headless (report: `scratch/web_stress/report.md`) |
| `data_crosscheck.py` | Are the saved files in `data/` right? Each index against an independent copy (FRED SP500, DJIA, NASDAQ100; Yahoo ^DJI for the MeasuringWorth Dow), the factor files against today's FRED, and the overlapping files against each other: missing days, wrong closes, return differences, and the app's numbers with each copy (downloads in `scratch/crosscheck/`; run with `python3 -I`) |
| `long_run_stability.py` | How often do the fitted settings run away over 100,000 days? |

Earlier exploration scripts (for the model before the November 2026 rebuild)
are in git history.

"""Can "panic" give the model the S&P 500's skew (falls bigger than rises)?

    python3 scripts/analysis/panic_skew.py          (about a minute on all cores)

The rebuilt model has no skew: its falls and rises are mirror images, while the S&P 500's big falls are
bigger than its big rises. Bouchaud, Matacz & Potters (2001, Phys. Rev. Lett. 87, 228701) explain the
"leverage effect" in indexes with panic: after falls, traders react more strongly. Here that is
model.simulate(panic=...): a falling trend pushes chartists to pessimism harder than a rising one pushes
them to optimism (U1 + panic / v1 * min(trend, 0); 0 = SPEC.md exactly).

For each panic weight, 10 held-out seeds of the S&P fit, S&P-length histories. Two skew measures:
skewness of the standardized returns, and the 1% quantile's size over the 99% quantile's (1.00 = mirror
images; above 1, the biggest falls are bigger than the biggest rises).

Result (Nov 2026): panic 0 -> 1.00, panic 10 (about 75 times the trend weight a2) -> 1.03; the S&P 500
is 1.09 (skewness -0.95 against the model's -0.05 to -0.34). Panic in the chartists' mood alone does not
give the market its skew: it only tilts who is a pessimist, and the fundamentalists pull the price back
just as hard either way. A real fix would need an asymmetry in how the price moves, not only in mood.
"""
import sys
from multiprocessing import Pool
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from herding import calibrate, explore as ex, market_data, model, stats  # noqa: E402

PANICS = (0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 7.0, 10.0)
SEEDS = calibrate.HELD_OUT_SEEDS[:10]


def skew_measures(r):
    """(skewness of the standardized returns, -1% quantile / 99% quantile)."""
    z = stats.standardize(r)
    lo, hi = np.quantile(z, [0.01, 0.99])
    return float(np.mean(z ** 3)), float(-lo / hi)


def one(job):
    panic, seed, p, burn, days = job
    try:
        out = model.simulate(p, days + burn, seed=seed, panic=panic)
    except model.RunawayError:
        return panic, None
    r = out["r"][burn:]
    return panic, (*skew_measures(r), float(stats.hill_alpha(r, 0.05)))


def main(panics=PANICS, seeds=SEEDS, days=None):
    p, burn = ex.fitted_settings()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns().values
    days = days or len(spx)
    s, q = skew_measures(spx)
    print(f"S&P 500: skewness {s:+.2f}, 1%/99% quantile ratio {q:.2f}")
    with Pool() as pool:
        res = pool.map(one, [(pv, sd, p, burn, days) for pv in panics for sd in seeds])
    rows = {}
    for pv in panics:
        ok = np.array([v for k, v in res if k == pv and v is not None])
        gone = sum(1 for k, v in res if k == pv and v is None)
        rows[pv] = (np.median(ok, axis=0) if len(ok) else None, gone)
        if len(ok):
            m = rows[pv][0]
            print(f"panic {pv:4.1f}: skewness {m[0]:+.2f}, quantile ratio {m[1]:.2f}, tail {m[2]:.2f}, "
                  f"ran away {gone} of {len(seeds)}")
        else:
            print(f"panic {pv:4.1f}: every history ran away")
    return rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""A formula with no traders: the GJR-GARCH(1,1) model, the standard way statisticians describe
volatility that comes in bursts (Bollerslev 1986, J. Econometrics 31:307-327; the GJR term for falls:
Glosten, Jagannathan & Runkle 1993, J. Finance 48:1779-1801).

Each day's return is r_t = mu + e_t, with e_t = s_t * z_t and z_t bell-curve noise (standard normal), and
    s_t^2 = omega + (alpha + gamma * [e_(t-1) < 0]) * e_(t-1)^2 + beta * s_(t-1)^2.
So a big move today makes tomorrow's typical move bigger (alpha), more so after a fall (gamma), and that
fades slowly (beta). Like the herding model it is fed only bell-curve news; unlike it there are no
traders: the bursts are written into the formula. The website uses it to ask whether herding explains
more than a formula does.

Fitted by maximum likelihood (the parameters that make the observed returns most probable).
"""
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

from .checks import is_number

NAMES = ("mu", "omega", "alpha", "gamma", "beta")


def _returns(r):
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    if r.ndim != 1 or r.size < 100 or not np.all(np.isfinite(r)):
        raise ValueError("need a 1-D list of at least 100 finite returns")
    return r


def variances(r, mu, omega, alpha, gamma, beta):
    """s_t^2 for each day of r (the first day starts from the sample variance of r)."""
    e = _returns(r) - mu
    s2 = np.empty_like(e)
    s2[0] = e.var()
    for t in range(1, e.size):
        s2[t] = omega + (alpha + gamma * (e[t - 1] < 0)) * e[t - 1] ** 2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
    return s2


def neg_loglik(theta, r):
    """Minus the log-likelihood of returns r under bell-curve z (the quantity fit() makes smallest)."""
    mu, omega, alpha, gamma, beta = theta
    s2 = variances(r, mu, omega, alpha, gamma, beta)
    e = r - mu
    return 0.5 * float(np.sum(np.log(2 * np.pi * s2) + e ** 2 / s2))


def _ok(theta):
    mu, omega, alpha, gamma, beta = theta
    return omega > 0 and alpha >= 0 and alpha + gamma >= 0 and beta >= 0 and alpha + gamma / 2 + beta < 1


def fit(r):
    """The GJR-GARCH(1,1) parameters (dict, NAMES) that fit returns r best."""
    r = _returns(r)
    v = r.var()
    start = np.array([r.mean(), 0.05 * v, 0.05, 0.05, 0.88])
    scale = np.array([r.std(), v, 1, 1, 1])        # optimise numbers of similar size

    def f(x):
        theta = x * scale
        return neg_loglik(theta, r) if _ok(theta) else 1e300

    best = minimize(f, start / scale, method="Nelder-Mead",
                    options=dict(maxiter=6000, xatol=1e-7, fatol=1e-7))
    best = minimize(f, best.x, method="Nelder-Mead", options=dict(maxiter=6000, xatol=1e-9, fatol=1e-9))
    theta = best.x * scale
    if not _ok(theta):
        raise ValueError("the fit did not find valid parameters")
    return dict(zip(NAMES, map(float, theta)))


def simulate(params, days, seed=None, burn=500):
    """`days` daily returns from GJR-GARCH(1,1) with these parameters and bell-curve z (after `burn`
    warm-up days, so the start doesn't matter). The same seed always gives the same returns."""
    if set(params) != set(NAMES) or not all(is_number(params[k]) for k in NAMES):
        raise ValueError(f"params must give the numbers {NAMES}, got {params!r}")
    if not _ok([params[k] for k in NAMES]):
        raise ValueError("params must have omega > 0, alpha >= 0, alpha + gamma >= 0, beta >= 0 and "
                         "alpha + gamma / 2 + beta < 1 (otherwise volatility grows without end)")
    if isinstance(days, bool) or not isinstance(days, (int, np.integer)) or days < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"days must be a whole number >= 1, got {days!r}")
    if isinstance(burn, bool) or not isinstance(burn, (int, np.integer)) or burn < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"burn must be a whole number >= 0, got {burn!r}")
    mu, omega, a, g, b = (params[k] for k in NAMES)
    z = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(int(days) + int(burn))
    s2 = omega / (1 - a - g / 2 - b)          # start at the long-run variance
    out = np.empty(z.size)
    for t in range(z.size):
        e = np.sqrt(s2) * z[t]
        out[t] = mu + e
        s2 = omega + (a + g * (e < 0)) * e * e + b * s2
    return out[int(burn):]

"""Tests of herding/garch.py (a formula with no traders) and the textbook checklist in herding/explore.py
(FACTS, fact_values, fact_passes, fact_table; Cont 2001), and of check 6 on the Checks page."""
import numpy as np
import pytest

from herding import explore as ex, garch, market_data
from test_web_pages import open_page  # noqa: F401

NUMS = ex.web_numbers()
SPX = market_data.spx_returns().values
TRUE = dict(mu=0.0003, omega=2e-6, alpha=0.03, gamma=0.1, beta=0.9)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ garch

# Spec: variances() is the recursion written out as a plain loop (it runs it with lfilter).
def test_variances_equal_a_plain_loop():
    r = garch.simulate(TRUE, 3000, seed=2)
    want = np.empty(r.size)
    e = r - TRUE["mu"]
    want[0] = e.var()
    for t in range(1, r.size):
        want[t] = (TRUE["omega"] + (TRUE["alpha"] + TRUE["gamma"] * (e[t - 1] < 0)) * e[t - 1] ** 2
                   + TRUE["beta"] * want[t - 1])
    assert garch.variances(r, *(TRUE[k] for k in garch.NAMES)) == pytest.approx(want, rel=1e-12)


# Spec: the log-likelihood by hand for 3 numbers: sum of log(2 pi s2) + e^2 / s2, halved, with a sign flip.
def test_neg_loglik_by_hand():
    r = np.r_[np.zeros(97), [0.01, -0.02, 0.005]]
    th = (0.0, 1e-5, 0.1, 0.05, 0.8)
    s2 = garch.variances(r, *th)
    want = 0.5 * np.sum(np.log(2 * np.pi * s2) + r ** 2 / s2)
    assert garch.neg_loglik(th, r) == pytest.approx(want, rel=1e-12)


# Spec: fitting data simulated from known settings gets them back. Tolerances from 20 other seeds
# (scratch check, Nov 2026: alpha within 0.012, gamma 0.03, beta 0.02 at 20,000 days); 2x that here.
@pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", [1, 7])
def test_fit_recovers_known_settings(seed):
    got = garch.fit(garch.simulate(TRUE, 20000, seed=seed))
    assert got["alpha"] == pytest.approx(TRUE["alpha"], abs=0.025)
    assert got["gamma"] == pytest.approx(TRUE["gamma"], abs=0.06)
    assert got["beta"] == pytest.approx(TRUE["beta"], abs=0.04)


# Spec: simulate repeats with the same seed; its long-run variance is omega / (1 - alpha - gamma/2 - beta).
def test_simulate_repeats_and_has_the_right_variance():
    a = garch.simulate(TRUE, 200000, seed=3)
    assert np.array_equal(a, garch.simulate(TRUE, 200000, seed=3))
    want = TRUE["omega"] / (1 - TRUE["alpha"] - TRUE["gamma"] / 2 - TRUE["beta"])
    assert a.var() == pytest.approx(want, rel=0.15)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("bad", [dict(TRUE, beta=0.99), dict(TRUE, omega=0.0), {"mu": 0}, dict(TRUE, mu="x")])
def test_simulate_rejects_bad_params(bad):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        garch.simulate(bad, 10)


def test_fit_rejects_bad_returns():
    for bad in ([0.1] * 10, np.r_[np.zeros(200), np.nan]):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            garch.fit(bad)


# Spec: the saved fit is the fit of the S&P 500 file (rerun it).
def test_saved_garch_fit_reruns():
    got = garch.fit(SPX)
    for k in garch.NAMES:
        assert got[k] == pytest.approx(NUMS["facts"]["garch_params"][k], rel=1e-9, abs=1e-12)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the checklist

# Spec: a plain bell curve passes only "no trend" and "tails thin out", as FACTS promises.
def test_a_bell_curve_passes_only_the_bell_curve_patterns():
    for seed in range(3):
        r = np.random.default_rng(seed).normal(0, 0.01, 20000)
        got = ex.fact_passes(ex.fact_values(r))
        assert {k for k, v in got.items() if v} <= {"no_trend", "thin_out"}, (seed, got)


# Spec: each measure by hand on a constructed series.
def test_fact_values_by_hand():
    r = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0, 0.01, 5000)
    v = ex.fact_values(r)
    z = (r - r.mean()) / r.std()
    lo, hi = np.quantile(z, [0.01, 0.99])
    assert v["skew"] == pytest.approx(-lo / hi, rel=1e-12)
    month = r[:5000].reshape(-1, 20).sum(axis=1)
    from herding import stats
    assert v["thin_out"] == pytest.approx(stats.kurtosis(month) - stats.kurtosis(r), rel=1e-12)
    e = r - r.mean()
    lev = np.mean([np.corrcoef(r[:-k], np.abs(e)[k:])[0, 1] for k in range(1, 11)])
    assert v["leverage"] == pytest.approx(lev, rel=1e-12)
    sd = np.array([np.sqrt(np.mean(e[t - 20:t] ** 2)) for t in range(20, r.size)])
    assert v["fat_in_calm"] == pytest.approx(stats.kurtosis(e[20:] / sd), rel=1e-9)


# Spec: a market whose falls are bigger passes "falls bigger than rises"; its mirror image does not.
def test_skew_rule_sees_bigger_falls():
    r = np.random.default_rng(2).standard_t(4, 20000) * 0.01
    r = np.where(r < 0, 1.3 * r, r)
    assert ex.fact_passes(ex.fact_values(r))["skew"]
    assert not ex.fact_passes(ex.fact_values(-r))["skew"]


def test_fact_values_rejects_short_or_bad():
    for bad in ([0.01] * 100, np.r_[np.zeros(600), np.inf]):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            ex.fact_values(bad)


# Spec: the S&P 500 passes every pattern (these are the patterns of real markets).
def test_the_sp500_passes_the_whole_checklist():
    assert all(ex.fact_passes(ex.fact_values(SPX)).values())


# Spec: the saved herding numbers rerun exactly for one held-out seed.
def test_saved_fact_values_rerun():
    p, burn = ex.fitted_settings()
    r, _ = ex.run_mix(p, "herding", p["a1"], NUMS["recipe"]["days"], NUMS["recipe"]["seeds"][0], burn)
    got = ex.fact_values(r)
    for k in ex.FACTS:
        assert got[k] == pytest.approx(NUMS["facts"]["herding"][k][0], rel=1e-12, abs=1e-15)
    g = garch.simulate(NUMS["facts"]["garch_params"], NUMS["recipe"]["days"], seed=NUMS["facts"]["garch_seeds"][0])
    got = ex.fact_values(g)
    for k in ex.FACTS:
        assert got[k] == pytest.approx(NUMS["facts"]["garch"][k][0], rel=1e-12, abs=1e-15)


# Spec: fact_table counts passes from the saved values (Nov 2026: herding 5, GARCH 6 of 8 in most histories).
def test_fact_table_counts():
    rows = ex.fact_table(NUMS, SPX)
    assert [r["key"] for r in rows] == list(ex.FACTS)
    for r in rows:
        test = ex.FACTS[r["key"]][3]
        assert r["herding_pass"] == sum(bool(test(v)) for v in NUMS["facts"]["herding"][r["key"]])
    assert sum(r["herding_pass"] > 20 for r in rows) == 5
    assert sum(r["garch_pass"] > 20 for r in rows) == 6


# Spec: the Checks page shows check 6 with one row per pattern and a scoreboard row.
def test_checks_page_shows_the_checklist(open_page):
    at = open_page("web/page_checks.py")
    assert not at.exception
    heads = [h.value for h in at.header]
    assert heads[5].startswith("6. The textbook checklist")
    table = at.table[1].value
    assert list(table.index) == [v[0] for v in ex.FACTS.values()]
    assert at.table[0].value.iloc[-1]["Verdict"] == "ℹ️ 5 of 8"

    r = garch.simulate(TRUE, 3000, seed=2)
    want = np.empty(r.size)

    for t in range(1, r.size):

weighted 3x, differential evolution (spx and paper), and the S&P from 1928 as the
  target. None passed the judging rule fixed in advance, so both settings files are
  unchanged (figures/RESULTS.md, "Overnight recalibration").

## Policy experiments (an extension, not in the sources; herding/policy.py)
Off by default; with both off the model is exactly sections 1-5.
- **Circuit breakers** (US rules since 2013, SEC-approved NYSE Rule 7.12, formerly
  Rule 80B): when the price falls 7% or 13% below the previous close **before 3:25 pm**
  (minute 355 of a 390-minute day, step 91 of 100), trading pauses for 15 minutes; a
  7% or 13% fall later in the day does nothing. At 20% it closes for the day, at any time. Each level fires at most once
  a day. "Paused" means the price is frozen: no ticks, while traders keep
  switching groups (their moods and strategies do not stop). Levels are scaled by
  (model daily sd / S&P daily sd), so 7% means the same number of typical days.
  Comparison: each seed is run with and without breakers. The two runs use the
  same random numbers until the first halt, so each history's first halt is a
  clean paired comparison (later days differ by chance too).
- **Policy surprise**: at the start of one day the fundamental value jumps by a
  fraction (here -10%), like an unexpected rate hike. The price's fall in units of
  the surprise is 1 - (change in log price - log value since the day before) / |ln(0.9)|:
  1 = the price followed the value exactly. A placebo (the same history without the
  surprise) measures how much of that the ordinary wobble gives by itself.

## Parameters
[L?] Parameter set I (unverified, from memory of [L] Table 1):
N=500, v1=3, v2=2, beta=6, T_c = N t_c = 10, T_f = N gamma = 5, a1=0.6, a2=0.2,
a3=0.5, p_f=10, r=0.004, R=0.0004, s=0.75, sigma_mu=0.05, sigma_eps=0.005.
Because these cannot be checked, the rebuild does not rely on them. Instead:
1. **Paper-matched settings:** fitted so the model reproduces [N]'s published numbers (below).

## Panic (an extension, not in the sources; model.simulate(panic=...))
Off by default (panic = 0: the term is exactly 0 and the model is sections 1-5). After Bouchaud,
Matacz & Potters (2001, Phys. Rev. Lett. 87, 228701), who explain the "leverage effect" of indexes
by panic: the chartists' mood index becomes
U1 = a1 x + (a2 / v1) (dp/dt)/p + (panic / v1) min((dp/dt)/p, 0),
so a falling trend pushes chartists to pessimism harder than a rising one pushes them to optimism.
Result (scripts/analysis/panic_skew.py, Nov 2026): it does not give the S&P 500's skew (the 1% worst
day over the 1% best day goes 1.00 -> 1.03 at panic 10; the S&P's is 1.09). It is not used on the website.

def sweep_at(nums, a1, tol=1e-9):
    """What the saved herding-strength sweep (numbers.json "sweep") says at one herding strength a1:
    {"a1", "n": histories, "ran_away": how many ran away, "tail": median tail exponent of the others
    (None if all ran away)}. ValueError if a1 is not one of the sweep's strengths."""
    rows = [r for r in nums["sweep"]["rows"] if abs(r["a1"] - a1) < tol]
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError(f"a1 = {a1!r} is not in the saved sweep")
    tails = [r["tail"] for r in rows if r["tail"] is not None]
    return {"a1": float(a1), "n": len(rows), "ran_away": len(rows) - len(tails),
            "tail": float(np.median(tails)) if tails else None}''',1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

def _log_run(new, res):
    """Put a run at the top of the run log. A run already in the log moves up instead of being
    added twice (pressing Run model again with the same settings gave duplicate rows)."""
    ss = st.session_state
    ss.log = [e for e in ss.log if e[1] != new]
    ss.log.insert(0, (datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S"), new, ex.mix_tails(res)))


def _run_log_table():
    """The run log with one number type per column: a run that ran away has no tail (empty), and the
    Ran away column says which mixes ran away (a text 'ran away' in a number column broke the table)."""
    ss = st.session_state
    out = []
    for t, prm, tl in ss.log:
        row = {"Time": t, "a1": prm["a1"], "a2": prm["a2"], "v1": prm["v1"],
               "Party drift (%/yr)": prm.get("party", 0.0), "Days": prm["days"], "Seed": prm["seed"]}
        # at a1 = 0 "chartists who herd" is the same history as "chartists, no herding": no second number
        shown = _shown_mixes(prm["a1"])
        row.update({c.MIX[m][0]: (np.nan if v is None or m not in shown else float(v)) for m, v in tl.items()})
        row["Ran away"] = ", ".join(c.MIX[m][0] for m, v in tl.items() if v is None and m in shown)
        out.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


def _run_log_view(df):
def _control_values():
    """The run the model controls describe now."""
    ss = st.session_state
    return {"a1": float(ss.in_a1), "a2": float(ss.in_a2), "v1": float(ss.in_v1),
            "days": int(ss.in_days), "seed": int(ss.in_seed), "party": float(ss.in_party)}


def _run(new):
    """Run the model with these settings (cached: a run made before comes back at once), put it in
    the run log and make it the run shown."""
    with st.spinner("Running the model..."):
        res = c.run_mixes(**new)
    _log_run(new, res)
    st.session_state.run = new


def _controls_changed():
    """True while a model control differs from the run shown, so the page can say Run model is needed."""
    ss = st.session_state
    return any(abs(float(ss[k]) - float(ss.run.get(p, 0.0))) > 1e-9 for k, p in SLIDERS)

def _init():
    ss = st.session_state
    ss.setdefault("asset", ("saved", "S&P 500"))
    ss.setdefault("ticker_error", "")
    ss.setdefault("ticker_error_for", None)        # the market on screen when the error was made
    ss.setdefault("run", c.default_run())
    _read_link()
    ss.setdefault("log", [])
    ss.setdefault("auto_run", True)                 # run the model as soon as a control changes
    # the tab follows the market on screen: a saved market's own tab; a live ticker keeps the tab open
    ss.setdefault("group", ex.market_group(ss.asset[1]) or "Indexes")
    # _load fell back to the S&P 500 after a run had drawn the ticker box: clear it now, before the
    # box is drawn (a widget's value can't be changed after it is drawn in the same run)
    if ss.pop("_fallback_done", False):
        ss.ticker_box = ""
        ss.group = "Indexes"
    if "party" not in ss.run:                   # a session from before the party drift existed
        ss.run = dict(ss.run, party=0.0)
    for k in ("a1", "a2", "v1", "days", "seed", "party"):

    # the preset picked is the one the controls match now, or none: a radio that kept showing
    # "S&P 500 fit" after a slider moved could not be clicked again to restore the fit
    ss.preset = _matching_preset()

def test_story_colors_and_wording(open_page):
    # PG-5: red (loss) marked an upward bubble and the +-4 sd lines; PG-10: "three index funds ... it never saw"
    at = open_page("web/page_story.py")

"""Tests of the Nov 2026 instructions (research: PhET, Stripe, Linear, Titan, Brilliant): the Test program's
three tasks with progress, its Try-this lines, presets that say what to expect (explore.sweep_at),
Reset everything; the Story's guess-then-reveal step; the Start here numbers and first steps. No chat box."""
import math

import numpy as np
import pytest

from conftest import ROOT
from herding import explore as ex
from test_web_explore_fixes import H, _group
from test_web_pages import app, open_page  # noqa: F401

NUMS = ex.web_numbers()
P, BURN = ex.fitted_settings()


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ sweep_at

# Spec: by hand from the saved rows: count the runaways and take the median of the other tails.
@pytest.mark.parametrize("a1", [0.0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.6, float(P["a1"])])
def test_sweep_at_by_hand(a1):
    rows = [r for r in NUMS["sweep"]["rows"] if abs(r["a1"] - a1) < 1e-9]
    tails = [r["tail"] for r in rows if r["tail"] is not None]
    got = ex.sweep_at(NUMS, a1)
    assert got["n"] == len(rows) == 10
    assert got["ran_away"] == len(rows) - len(tails)
    assert got["tail"] == (float(np.median(tails)) if tails else None)


def test_sweep_at_rejects_strengths_not_saved():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        ex.sweep_at(NUMS, 0.7)


# Spec: the science the instructions teach: runaways fall and the tail exponent rises (calmer) as
# herding grows, in the saved sweep, wherever at least half the histories survive.
def test_more_herding_is_calmer_in_the_saved_sweep():
    a1s = sorted({r["a1"] for r in NUMS["sweep"]["rows"]})
    at = [ex.sweep_at(NUMS, a) for a in a1s]
    gone = [w["ran_away"] for w in at]
    assert all(x >= y for x, y in zip(gone, gone[1:]))
    tails = [w["tail"] for w in at if w["ran_away"] <= w["n"] / 2]
    assert tails[0] < 3.1 < tails[-1] and tails[-1] > 4


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Test program

# Spec: each preset's note is the sweep's numbers in words.
def test_preset_notes_say_what_to_expect(app):
    at = app()
    notes = list(at.sidebar.radio[0].proto.captions)
    assert notes[0] == f"a1 = {P['a1']:.2f}: tail about {ex.sweep_at(NUMS, P['a1'])['tail']:.1f} (like the S&P 500)"
    assert notes[1] == "a1 = 1.60: tail about 4.7 (calm: thin tails)"
    assert notes[2] == "a1 = 0.60: runs away in 9 of 10; wild when it doesn't"
    assert notes[3] == "a1 = 0.00: runs away in all 10 saved histories"


# Spec: the tasks tick only when really done: zoom to the biggest crash; run at a1 <= 0.8.
def test_tasks_tick_as_they_are_done(app):
    at = app()
    assert at.expander[0].label == "Three things to try · 0 of 3 done"
    _group(at, "view").set_value("Model market").run()
    _group(at, "mm_zoom").set_value("burst").run()
    assert at.expander[0].label == "Three things to try · 0 of 3 done"      # the wrong zoom doesn't count
    _group(at, "mm_zoom").set_value("crash").run()
    assert at.expander[0].label == "Three things to try · 1 of 3 done"
    at.slider(key="in_a1").set_value(0.81).run()
    assert at.expander[0].label == "Three things to try · 1 of 3 done"      # 0.81 is not the edge
    at.slider(key="in_a1").set_value(0.8).run()
    assert at.expander[0].label == "Three things to try · 2 of 3 done"
    assert not at.exception


# Spec: the challenge needs another seed AND the herding tail within 0.10 of the S&P 500's.
def test_challenge_rule():
    import streamlit as st
    ss = st.session_state
    spx = {"tail": 2.92}
    for seed, tail, want in ((1000, 2.95, False), (7, 2.95, True), (7, 3.05, False), (7, 2.82, True)):
        ss.clear()
        ss.run = dict(seed=seed)
        ss.log = []
        got = H["_tasks_done"]("S&P 500", spx, {"herding": {"tail": tail}})
        assert got[2] is want, (seed, tail)
    ss.clear()
    ss.run, ss.log = dict(seed=7), []
    assert H["_tasks_done"]("Apple", spx, {"herding": {"tail": 2.92}})[2] is False   # on the S&P 500 only
    ss.clear()


# Spec: Reset everything goes back to the S&P 500 and the fitted settings, and keeps the run log.
def test_reset_everything(app):
    at = app()
    at.slider(key="in_a1").set_value(1.5).run()
    n_log = len(at.session_state["log"])
    at.sidebar.button[0].click().run()
    assert at.session_state["in_a1"] == pytest.approx(float(P["a1"]), abs=1e-12)
    assert at.session_state["asset"] == ("saved", "S&P 500")
    assert len(at.session_state["log"]) >= n_log
    assert not at.exception


# Spec: every chart view has a Try-this line, and it names the market on screen where it says {name}.
def test_every_view_has_a_try_line():
    assert set(H["TRY"]) == set(H["VIEWS"])
    assert "{name}" in H["TRY"]["Tail"]


# Spec: no chat box anywhere on the site (the owner's rule: no AI usage on a public site).
def test_no_chat_box_on_any_page():
    for f in [ROOT / "app.py", *sorted((ROOT / "web").glob("*.py"))]:
        text = f.read_text()
        assert "chat_input" not in text and "chat_message" not in text and "anthropic" not in text.lower(), f


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Story

# Spec: the chart of step 5 is hidden until a guess (or Just show me); each guess gets its verdict.
def test_story_guess_then_reveal(open_page):
    at = open_page("web/page_story.py")
    assert not at.exception
    keys = [pc.proto.id for pc in at.get("plotly_chart")]
    assert not any(k.endswith("-s5") for k in keys)
    at.button(key="story_show").click().run()
    assert any(pc.proto.id.endswith("-s5") for pc in at.get("plotly_chart"))
    at = open_page("web/page_story.py")
    at.get("button_group")[0].set_value("Calmer and calmer").run()
    text = " ".join(m.value for m in at.markdown)
    assert "Yes, surprisingly" in text and "runs away in all 10" in text


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ Start here

# Spec: the three numbers are computed: 10^86, the S&P record in years, the model's 8-sd wait.
def test_start_here_numbers(open_page):
    at = open_page(None)
    assert not at.exception
    vals = [m.value for m in at.metric]
    assert vals[0] == f"10^{math.floor(math.log10(ex.bell_crash_years(20)))} years" == "10^86 years"
    assert vals[1] == "77 years" and vals[2] == "35 years"
    assert "The full manual: every button and chart" in [e.label for e in at.expander]

**Core idea saved to memory.** Every session now opens with your proposal's question: does bell-curve news plus herding alone make crashes, fat tails and clustering? It also carries the no-chat-box rule.

## What the research found
I sent out two helpers. One studied 10 Y Combinator fintech companies (Alpaca, Kalshi, Groww, AlgoTest, Titan and others). The other studied tech and learning sites (Stripe, Linear, Duolingo, TradingView, Fidelity, and PhET's published simulation design rules). The patterns I used:
- **The idea as the headline** (AlgoTest).
- **Numbered first tasks** (Titan, Linear).
- **Presets that say what to expect** (Stripe's test tables).
- **One action, then a safe Reset** (PhET).
- **Guess, then reveal** (Brilliant, NYT).
- **Number-first cards** (Fidelity, Groww).

I left out trading or "start investing" framing, hype counters, and every AI or chat feature those sites have.

## What changed
**A. Instructions**
- **Start here:**
  - The headline is your question.
  - Three number cards: a bell curve's wait for a 20-sd fall is 10^86 years; the real S&P 500's was 77 years; the herding model has an 8-sd fall about every 35 years.
  - A "first five minutes" path. The long manual is now a fold-out.
- **Test program:**
  - A "Three things to try" card that ticks off as you go: watch a crash, find the edge, and a challenge.
  - A "Try this" line under every chart.
  - Presets that say what to expect, and a Reset button.
- **Story:** a new step 5. You guess whether more herding makes the market wilder or calmer, then the chart answers.

**B. Speed.** These changes leave every result the same.
- A slider move in the Simulated market view went from 0.93 s to 0.55 s.
- The server prepares the Story and Findings pages when it starts.
- Data sent to the browser is compressed, about 4× smaller.

**C. Science.** New check 6 on the Checks page: the textbook checklist of real-market patterns (Cont 2001), compared with GARCH, a formula with no traders.
- The S&P 500 passes all 8 patterns.
- Your herding model passes 5; GARCH passes 6 (one of those only by 21 histories of 40).
- Herding doesn't beat the formula on the numbers. What it adds is a *reason* the patterns appear.

## Two findings you should know about
1. **More herding makes the market calmer, not wilder.** With too little copying it runs away; with a lot it goes calm (tail 4.7 at a1 = 1.6). The S&P-like tail of about 3 appears only near the runaway edge, which is the "criticality" in Lux and Marchesi's title. "Strong herding" is the *calm* preset, and the site now says so.
2. **Panic doesn't fix the missing skew.** I added an optional "panic" term (Bouchaud 2001) that makes traders react harder to falls. Even at its strongest it only reaches 1.03 on the skew measure, against the S&P's 1.09. So it isn't on the site; `scripts/analysis/panic_skew.py` reproduces the result and SPEC.md documents it.

input.prompt:
Research task only. Do NOT edit any project files. Notes, if any, only under /Users/avishjain/02-120 Project/scratch/ (never /tmp).

Project (keep central): a student Streamlit + Plotly web app (/Users/avishjain/02-120 Project; app.py, pages in web/, colors and CSS in web/common.py: PALETTES, css(), style(), the terminal-style "tape" header) asking "if news is plain bell-curve noise, does herding among traders alone create the fat tails, crashes and volatility clustering of real markets?" (Lux-Marchesi 1999 model vs the S&P 500). The owner LIKES the current boxy, terminal-like trading look (monospace labels, bordered boxes, a ticker tape) and wants to keep it, but says the charts are not clear enough in light and dark mode, and wants the site usable by a wider audience (older people, beginners, phones, colorblind users). No chat box / no AI features.

Visit real trading/market sites and take concrete notes (public pages, product pages, help-center screenshots, design blog posts; say which couldn't load): TradingView (chart page and its light/dark themes), Robinhood (web + their published design notes, e.g. "Robinhood design" blog), Webull, Coinbase (and its open-source design system "Coinbase Design System" docs if public), Kraken Pro, Koyfin, Finviz, Bloomberg Terminal (articles on its design: "How Bloomberg Terminal UX designers conceal complexity", Bloomberg's accessible color work for colorblind users), Yahoo Finance quote page, Google Finance, Interactive Brokers' accessibility notes. Also check Plotly/Streamlit-feasible chart-readability guidance: line widths, gridline contrast, crosshair/hover behavior, number formatting, legend placement, colorblind-safe up/down colors (e.g. Bloomberg/TradingView options for blue/orange instead of green/red).

Report (under 900 words):
1. For each site, 1-2 lines on what makes its charts readable and its layout calm (spacing, type size, contrast, how much is shown at once).
2. Scrolling and motion: what they animate (price tick flashes, number count-ups, chart draw-in, sticky headers that shrink on scroll, skeleton loaders), how subtle, and which respect "reduced motion". Rank 5-8 motion/scroll ideas that are feasible in Streamlit (CSS via st.html with @keyframes, position: sticky, prefers-reduced-motion; Plotly transitions) with how to build each and risk (Streamlit reruns re-trigger animations; keep it subtle).
3. Chart clarity: 8-10 concrete rules to apply to our Plotly charts in BOTH light and dark (line widths, contrast targets, gridline opacity, axis label size, crosshair spikelines, unified vs closest hover, max lines per chart, direct labels instead of legends, colorblind-safe palette pairs), each tied to a source site.
4. Accessibility for a wider audience: font size minimums, contrast (WCAG 2.2 AA 4.5:1 text, 3:1 graphics), touch target sizes, plain-language tooltips — with sources.
5. Three things NOT to copy (dense pro-trader clutter, gamified confetti, etc.).

input.prompt:
Audit task only. Do NOT edit project files. Throwaway scripts and screenshots only under /Users/avishjain/02-120 Project/scratch/chart_audit/ (never /tmp). Don't run the full test suite.

Project: Streamlit + Plotly app in /Users/avishjain/02-120 Project. Colors, chart style and CSS are in web/common.py (PALETTES with "light" and "dark", MIX colors for the three trader mixes, css(), style(fig,...), template building, tail_chart, dial_chart, show()). Pages: web/page_guide.py, page_story.py, page_explore.py (biggest: price chart _price_chart, _model_market_chart, histogram/tail/bursts/memory charts), page_compare.py, page_checks.py, page_findings.py. Light/dark switch: .streamlit/config.toml has both themes. The owner says the charts are not clear enough in dark and light mode and wants a wider audience (older people, colorblind users, phones) to read them. The boxy terminal look must stay.

Do:
1. Compute WCAG contrast ratios for every palette color used for chart lines, markers, fills, gridlines, axis text and hover text against each mode's chart background (BG/CARD/PANEL as actually used by style()/the template). Flag lines/markers under 3:1 and text under 4.5:1. Note which fills (HERD_FILL, OK_FILL, etc.) make overlaid lines hard to see.
2. Check colorblind safety: simulate deuteranopia/protanopia/tritanopia (e.g. with a simple Machado or Brettel matrix in numpy) for the pairs that must be told apart on the same chart: UP vs DOWN, REAL vs BELL vs the three MIX colors, model vs S&P lines. Report pairs whose simulated colors are too close (deltaE or contrast).
3. Read the chart code and list concrete clarity problems: line widths under ~1.5 px for main series, dotted lines carrying important data, too many traces per chart, legends far from lines, tiny fonts (Plotly font size < 12), hover modes, gridline contrast, log axes without readable ticks, annotations overlapping, charts too short on phones (heights), thin() downsampling making lines jagged.
4. Optionally render a few charts to PNG with plotly+kaleido if installed (check; don't install), or take screenshots of the running site at http://localhost:8501 if it's up (pages /, /page_story, /page_explore, /page_checks) using nothing heavier than what's installed; if you can't render, say so and rely on the numbers.

Report (under 700 words): a table of the worst 10 problems (where, measured number, why it hurts readability, concrete fix with exact new values: colors as hex with their new contrast ratio, widths, font sizes), ordered by impact; then a proposed revised palette for light and dark (hex values, each with contrast vs background and a colorblind note) that keeps the current boxy terminal feel. Results must not change any computed number — styling only.

input.description: Audit site features against proposal
input.prompt:
Audit task only. Do NOT edit project files. Notes only under /Users/avishjain/02-120 Project/scratch/ (never /tmp).

The project's proposal (docs/proposal.pdf in /Users/avishjain/02-120 Project; read it with pypdf: python3 -c "import pypdf; print(''.join(p.extract_text() for p in pypdf.PdfReader('docs/proposal.pdf').pages))"). Its core: "if the news is normally distributed, does herding create fat tails and the volatility ranges seen in markets?" Black Monday should not happen in 10^86 years under a bell curve; show crashes happen within decades. Build: first replicate Kirman's ant model against his math; then the Lux-Marchesi model (500 traders switching between fundamentalists and herding chartists), compared side by side with real S&P 500 data; a web app where people adjust the amount and strength of herding and watch crashes and how they cluster. Checks: extreme moves and volatility vs the S&P 500; zero chartists -> bell curve; tail exponent about 2.6-3 with chartists. Beyond the paper: fix weaknesses.

The site (Streamlit): app.py and web/page_guide.py (Start here), page_story.py (Story, 6 steps), page_explore.py (Test program: market picker with indexes/stocks/commodities and any Yahoo ticker, live prices and intraday 1D/7D, range buttons, views Price/Simulated market/Tail/Histogram/Bursts/Memory, president's-party shading and party drift slider, model controls a1/a2/v1/days/seed, presets, run log, shareable links, big-day reader, scorecard, dial chart, tasks card), page_compare.py (Compare: all markets on one map), page_checks.py (6 checks + scoreboard), page_findings.py (figures, party table, paper comparison). Shared: web/common.py (live quotes ticker tape, FRED backup, etc.). Read the pages' code (skim; focus on what the visitor sees) and, if it is running, look at http://localhost:8501 (paths /, /page_story, /page_explore, /page_compare, /page_checks, /page_findings) with whatever you have (requests/AppTest is fine: streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest.from_file('app.py').run(), then switch_page).

Produce, for the owner (a beginner who wants the site as close to the proposal as possible and usable by a wide audience):
1. An inventory: every visible feature/control/chart per page, one line each.
2. For each: KEEP (core to the proposal), REDEFINE (keep but simplify/rename/merge — say how), MOVE (to a fold-out "Extras" or Findings), or CUT (off-topic or duplicate), with a one-line reason tied to the proposal text. Be decisive. Candidates to scrutinize: president's party shading/drift (an extension unrelated to herding), commodities and 20 stocks, live/intraday prices, Compare page vs Checks overlap, Findings vs Checks overlap, a2/v1/party in model settings, run log, dial chart, shareable links, six chart views (too many?), the 6-step Story vs Start here duplication, the "amount of herding" in the proposal (no control maps to it directly; the chartist share is shown in Simulated market).
3. A proposed simpler site map (pages and what's on each, in order) that follows the proposal's own order: question -> Kirman check -> model -> side by side with S&P -> tune herding and watch crashes cluster -> checks -> beyond the paper.
4. Risks: what cutting would break (tests in tests/ that would need changing — grep for key names), and anything in the proposal the site still doesn't do.
Under 900 words, plain language.

  **Site audit against the proposal**
  
  I read the proposal and the code for all six pages. The server answers at localhost:8501, but I did not click through it in a browser, so what visitors see is taken from the code. I edited no files.
  
  **1–2. Inventory and verdicts**
  
  **Start here (page_guide.py)**
  - Title and lead paragraph: KEEP. This is the proposal's question.
  - Three numbers: a bell curve's 10^N-year wait vs the S&P's real wait vs the model's wait: KEEP. This is the "10^86 years vs decades" claim.
  - "First five minutes" cards and the short-answer box: REDEFINE. Shrink to a single "Start the story" button.
  - "What the model is": KEEP.
  - Full manual expander: MOVE to Extras. It mostly documents features that would be cut.
  - How to read the charts, with an example tail chart: MOVE into the Story, at the first place a tail chart appears.
  - Controls list and glossary: REDEFINE into one short glossary that every page links to.
  - Things to keep in mind, and Run it yourself: KEEP as a footer.
  
  **Story (page_story.py, 6 steps)**
  - Step 1, too many big days on the S&P 500: KEEP.
  - Step 2, value traders alone give a bell curve: KEEP. This is the zero-chartists base case.
  - Step 3, trend-followers alone run away: KEEP.
  - Step 4, add herding to get fat tails and bursts: KEEP.
  - Step 5, the "guess" quiz on how much herding: KEEP. It is the closest thing to the proposal's "amount of herding".
  - Step 6, try it yourself: REDEFINE into a link to the Lab.
  - Missing: the Story never mentions Kirman. The proposal does Kirman first, but the site shows it only as check 1 on the Checks page.
  
  **Test program (page_explore.py)**
  - Market picker, Indexes tab (S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow): KEEP, but default to the S&P 500. The proposal compares only against the S&P.
  - Stocks tab (20 stocks) and Commodities tab: MOVE to Extras. They are not in the proposal.
  - "Type any ticker" box: MOVE to Extras.
  - Live prices switch, 1D/7D within-day prices, live quote: CUT. Herding tails need decades of daily data, so live prices don't help answer the question.
  - Ticker tape at the top of every page (from common.tape): CUT. It looks like a finance terminal, not a science project.
  - Range buttons YTD to All: REDEFINE to All, 20Y and 5Y only.
  - Six chart views. REDEFINE to four:
    - Simulated market: rename it "Watch a crash".
    - Tail: rename it "How rare big days are".
    - Bursts: keep it; this is where visitors watch crashes cluster.
    - Merge Histogram into Tail as a toggle.
    - Merge Memory into Bursts.
    - Move Price to Extras.
  - Price toggles (Big days, drawdown, log scale): MOVE to Extras with the Price view.
  - Big-day reader: MOVE to Extras. It is fun but not the question.
  - President's party shading and party panel: CUT from this page. It is an extension unrelated to herding; it already lives on Findings.
  - Herding strength (a1) slider: KEEP. This is "the strength of herding".
  - A2 and v1 sliders: MOVE into an "Advanced" fold-out. They are not in the proposal's vocabulary.
  - Party drift slider: CUT. It sits among the model settings and suggests politics is part of the model.
  - Days and seed: KEEP, inside Advanced.
  - Model presets (fit, strong, weak, none): REDEFINE into the main "amount of herding" control: "None / Some / Fitted / Strong", shown next to a1.

  **Research report: how trading sites keep charts readable and calm, and what to borrow for the herding web app** (nothing in the project was edited; no notes were saved)
  
  **What I could and couldn't see**
  - **Looked at in the browser:** TradingView's chart page (light theme, SPX) and Yahoo Finance's ^GSPC quote page.
  - **Read as text only:** Finviz, Webull, Robinhood's help article "Using charts", Coinbase Design System's LineChart docs, and Interactive Brokers' accessibility FAQ and policy.
  - **Blocked or empty:**
    - Every Bloomberg page refused automated reading (HTTP 403), including "How Bloomberg Terminal UX designers conceal complexity" and the color-accessibility post. I only have their search summaries.
    - Google Finance showed "device not supported".
    - Coinbase's accessibility page had no rules on it.
    - Koyfin's blog has no posts on chart design.
    - For Kraken Pro I found only product blog posts.
    - I found no official Robinhood design blog. Robinhood material comes from a Bloomberg 2021 feature and a Google Design case study, again via search summaries.
  
  **1. What each site does**
  - **TradingView:**
    - Very faint grid. The price and the last-price tag sit on the right axis in the series color.
    - The open/high/low/close values are a one-line text legend at top left. Volume is desaturated in the background.
    - Time-range buttons (1D…All) sit under the chart.
    - Body text is 14px in a system font. The page title uses a ▼ arrow and a true minus sign ("−0.25%").
  - **Yahoo Finance:**
    - One area line with a dotted previous-close reference line, and the last price tagged on the axis.
    - A sticky header, and a market strip of small sparklines. Body text is 14px.
    - Its CSS has a prefers-reduced-motion rule.
  - **Robinhood:** one line per chart, green or red for the whole graph, and scrub-to-read. Its help page explains charts in plain words ("large swings… indicate a volatile price").
  - **Webull:** a 10-stat grid with range buttons. There is no glossary for P/E, turnover and similar terms.
  - **Finviz:** roughly 80–90 label/value fields plus promo banners. This is maximum density.
  - **Coinbase Design System:**
    - Line widths of 2–3px in its examples.
    - A "scrubber" (a cursor that follows your finger along the line) that labels each series beside it.
    - Gain/loss text labels, so color is never the only cue.
    - A label you can set per chart for screen readers, and `animate={false}` to switch animation off.
  - **Bloomberg:**
    - Hides complexity instead of removing it, and treats consistency as a method ("even a font swap… can throw users off").
    - About 20,000 users have color-vision deficiency, and red and green look alike to them. The command PDFU COLORS offers schemes for deuteranopia and protanomaly. I could not confirm that blue/orange is one of them.
  - **Interactive Brokers:** Client Portal colors meet WCAG 2.0 AA contrast, text can be resized without losing content, and it cites EN 301 549.
  
  **2. Motion and scrolling, ranked for Streamlit**

  3. **Pause control on the ticker tape, if it scrolls.** WCAG 2.2.2 requires a pause/stop for anything that moves on its own for more than 5 s.   6. **Plotly `layout.transition` (300 ms, cubic-in-out) for the herding-strength sweep.** It often does nothing, because `st.plotly_chart` and fragments redraw the chart from scratch. Treat it as optional. Medium risk.
  7. **Loading placeholders.** `st.spinner` or `st.status` while a simulation runs, instead of a custom shimmer animation. Low value.
  8. **Avoid number count-ups.** Coinbase has a RollingNumber component, but in-between values of a tail exponent would mislead readers.

  I measured contrast against the CARD color.
  1. **Line widths:** data lines 2–2.5px, reference lines 1–1.5px dashed (Coinbase CDS). `mix_line` at 2.2 is fine.
  2. **Gridlines:** horizontal only, faint but visible, about 1.3–1.6:1.
     - Dark GRID `#1C1C1C` is 1.2:1, effectively invisible.
     - Light GRID is 1.27:1.
     - Raising both slightly makes the grid readable while staying calm (TradingView, Yahoo).
  3. **Contrast of lines and marks:** every line or mark should be at least 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11). Currently below or just at the limit:
     - Light: PICK `#B58900` 3.21, SHADE_LOW 3.09, chartists `#C77700` 3.46, GUIDE 3.36.
     - Dark: GUIDE 3.17.
     - Darken these toward 4:1 or more.

  5. **Colorblind-safe pairs:** keep the current blue/orange/pink set, already Okabe-Ito (a standard colorblind-safe palette). Never rely on red vs green alone. PICK_DASH as a second cue is the right idea.

     - Raise `hoverlabel` text to 13–14px.

     - Put the series name and last value at the line's right end, in its color (TradingView's axis tag, Coinbase's labels beside the scrubber).

  - **Font sizes:** body text 16px minimum for older readers. Both pro sites use 14px, which is fine for traders but not for this audience. Nothing smaller than 12px anywhere.
  - **Zoom and phones:** must survive 200% zoom (1.4.4) and reflow at 320px width with no sideways scrolling (1.4.10). IBKR advertises text resizing.
  - **Touch targets:** at least 24×24px (WCAG 2.5.8 AA). Aim for 44×44 (2.5.5 AAA, Apple's guideline) on buttons, range chips and the theme toggle.
  - **Motion:** pause control for auto-moving content (2.2.2), and honor reduced motion (2.3.3).
  - **Plain-language help:**
    - Explain like Robinhood's help page, not Webull or Finviz, which leave jargon undefined.
    - Attach the existing `HELP` entries as "?" help on every metric.
    - Hover tooltips don't exist on phones, so also show a one-line caption.
    - Give each chart a sentence saying what to notice. This is the Streamlit version of Coinbase's screen-reader label.
  
  **5. Three things not to copy**
  1. **Pro-trader density:** Finviz's ~85 fields; TradingView's 20+ tool icons, promo pop-ups and AI callouts; Kraken's eight charts per screen.
  2. **Gamified, emotional motion:** Robinhood's real-time green/red flashing and its celebration effects, which the Bloomberg 2021 feature linked to gamification (the confetti detail is my memory; the summary only described the flashing). TradingView's Black Friday countdown with seconds ticking.
  3. **Candlesticks and red/green as the only signal:** they are jargon for beginners and fail for colorblind readers. Keep line charts with labeled direction.

content.text:
I've finished the research and changed nothing yet. Three helpers looked into it: one studied trading sites (TradingView, Yahoo Finance, Robinhood, Coinbase's design system, Webull, Finviz, Interactive Brokers), one measured your charts in light and dark mode, and one checked every feature against your proposal. Bloomberg's and Google Finance's pages blocked automated reading, so their notes come from summaries only.

Every item below is numbered, so you can approve a whole group or strike single items, like "all of 2, skip 1c." None of it changes any computed result.

## 1. Cut or redefine, to match your proposal
- **1a. Kirman goes first.** Your proposal reproduces Kirman's ants before the market model, but the site only shows them as check 1 on the Checks page. I'd add the live ant chart as the first step of the Story.
- **1b. Move the president's-party material out of the Test program.** The shading, the party panel and the "party drift" slider aren't about herding, and the slider makes politics look like part of the model. The party analysis stays on Findings, labelled "Extension."
- **1c. Move other markets into an "Other markets" fold-out.** That means stocks, commodities, typed tickers and live within-day prices. Your proposal compares the model with the S&P 500 only, but you asked for live Yahoo prices earlier, so I'd move these rather than delete them. The ticker tape stays, since it's part of the boxy look you like.
- **1d. Six chart views become four:** Price, Watch a crash (now "Simulated market"), How rare big days are (with the histogram as a switch inside it), and Wild-day bursts (with volatility memory underneath).
- **1e. Simpler controls:**
  - Remove the run log; the "every run on one chart" view already shows every run.
  - Runs always happen automatically, so the Run model button and its switch go.
  - a2, v1, days and seed stay in "Advanced."
- **1f. Merge the Compare page into Findings as "Beyond the paper,"** together with check 6 (the textbook checklist vs the formula with no traders).
- **1g. Say plainly what "amount of herding" means.** No control sets how many traders become chartists; the market decides that itself. The site should say: "you set how strongly traders copy; how many become chartists is up to the market."
- **1h. Trim Start here** to the question, the three numbers, what the model is, and one button. The manual covers features that move, so it shrinks.

## 2. Clearer charts (measured problems, fixes keep the boxy look)
- **2a. New colors in both modes.** In light mode, red-green colorblind visitors see the herding line and the bell-curve line as the same gray, and that's the main comparison. With the new colors, every line reaches at least 3:1 contrast and every colored label 4.5:1.
- **2b. Thicker lines.** Main data lines go from 1 px to 1.6 px, which fixes the jagged look.
- **2c. Visible gridlines and guides.** The ±4-standard-deviation guides currently disappear behind the data.
- **2d. Fundamentalists drawn dash-dot.** They're currently dotted, the same as the bell curve, and the two lines overlap.
- **2e. Text size 12 at least, 13 on phones.** Some labels are 10–11 now.
- **2f. Taller charts and shorter legends on phones.** On a phone the legend currently takes about 20% of a chart.
- **2g. A vertical guide line under your cursor on time charts** (TradingView style). Both "Bursts" panels also get the same scale; right now they're scaled differently, which makes the bursts look different in size.

## 3. Look and motion (borrowed from Yahoo, TradingView and Coinbase; subtle only)
- **3a. The ticker tape stays at the top while you scroll.**
- **3b. A brief color flash when a live price actually changes,** with a ▲/▼ arrow.
- **3c. A quick fade-in for new results** (under 0.2 s).
- **3d. A true minus sign (−) and an up/down arrow** on every colored change, so color is never the only cue.
- **3e. All motion switches off** for visitors whose device is set to reduce motion.

I'm leaving out confetti, number count-ups, candlesticks and pro-trader clutter.

## 4. Easier for older visitors and phone users
- **4a. Body text 16 px.**
- **4b. Buttons and chips at least 44 px tall.**
- **4c. A "?" with a plain-language explanation on every number, plus a one-line caption under each chart,** because hover tooltips don't work on phones.

Two honest notes:
- Group 1 changes the most, and about 150 tests are tied to these features. I'd update those tests carefully, without weakening them.
- Groups 2–4 are styling only.

"""Real numbers for the mock-up page (scratch/mockup/index.html): writes scratch/mockup/data.js."""
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from herding import explore as ex, kirman

def thin(x, y, n=1200):
    i = ex.thin_indices(np.asarray(y, float), n)
    return [x[j] for j in i], [float(y[j]) for j in i]

close = ex.saved_prices("S&P 500")
r = ex.log_returns(close)
s = ex.summary(r.values)
p, burn = ex.fitted_settings()
nums = ex.web_numbers()
days = len(r)
seed = int(nums["recipe"]["seeds"][0])
out = {"spx": {"tail": s["tail"], "kurt": s["kurtosis"], "memory": s["memory"], "big": s["big_days"],
               "bell_big": s["bell_big_days"], "last": float(close.iloc[-1]),
               "chg": float(close.iloc[-1] / close.iloc[-2] - 1), "date": close.index[-1].strftime("%d %b %Y")}}
dates = [d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") for d in close.index]
out["price"] = dict(zip(("x", "y"), thin(dates, close.values)))
big = ex.big_day_list(r)
out["big"] = {"x": [d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") for d in big.index], "y": [float(close.loc[d]) for d in big.index],
              "move": [float(m) for m in big["move"]]}
xs, ys = ex.tail_curve(r.values)
out["tail_spx"] = {"x": list(map(float, xs)), "y": list(map(float, ys))}
grid = np.geomspace(0.1, 30, 120)
out["bell"] = {"x": list(map(float, grid)), "y": list(map(float, ex.bell_tail(grid)))}
zs = ex.moves_in_sd(r.values)
out["bursts_spx"] = dict(zip(("x", "y"), thin(dates[1:], zs)))
runs = {}
for a1 in (0.9, round(float(p["a1"]), 2), 1.4):
    m = ex.run_mixes(p, burn, a1, p["a2"], p["v1"], days, seed)
    herd, fund = m["herding"][0], m["fundamentalists"][0]
    entry = {"a1": a1, "ran": m["herding"][1]}
    if herd is not None:
        sm = ex.summary(herd)
        tx, ty = ex.tail_curve(herd)
        zh = ex.moves_in_sd(herd)
        bx, by = thin(list(range(len(zh))), zh)
        entry.update(tail=sm["tail"], kurt=sm["kurtosis"], memory=sm["memory"], big=sm["big_days"],
                     tail_x=list(map(float, tx)), tail_y=list(map(float, ty)), burst_x=bx, burst_y=by,
                     score=ex.scorecard(s, sm))
    runs[str(a1)] = entry
fx, fy = ex.tail_curve(m["fundamentalists"][0])
out["tail_fund"] = {"x": list(map(float, fx)), "y": list(map(float, fy))}
out["runs"] = runs
out["fit_a1"] = round(float(p["a1"]), 2)
mm = ex.model_market(p, burn, "herding", float(p["a1"]), p["a2"], p["v1"], days, seed)
a, b = ex.zoom_window(mm["r"], "crash")
out["crash"] = {"first": a, "day": list(range(a, b + 1)), "price": mm["price"][a:b + 1].tolist(),
                "value": mm["value"][a:b + 1].tolist(), "z": mm["z"][a:b + 1].tolist(),
                "crowd": (mm["z"] * mm["x"])[a:b + 1].tolist()}
k = kirman.simulate(100, 0.002, 0.1, 20_000_000, seed=1)
sim, exact, tv = ex.kirman_match(k, 100, 0.002, 0.1)
st, ct = ex.kirman_path(k)
out["kirman"] = {"steps": (np.asarray(st) / 1e6).tolist(), "count": np.asarray(ct).tolist(),
                 "sim": list(map(float, sim)), "exact": list(map(float, exact)), "tv": float(tv)}
cc = ex.crash_check(nums, r.values)
out["crash_years"] = {"model8": cc["row"]["model"], "bm_model": cc["bm_model"], "spx_years": days / 252}
facts = ex.fact_table(nums, r.values)
out["checks"] = {"tail_median": ex.spread(nums["checks"]["herding"]["tail"])["median"],
                 "kurt_median": ex.spread(nums["checks"]["fundamentalists"]["kurtosis"])["median"],
                 "herd_facts": sum(f["herding_pass"] > 20 for f in facts),
                 "garch_facts": sum(f["garch_pass"] > 20 for f in facts)}
(Path(__file__).parent / "data.js").write_text("window.MOCK = " + json.dumps(out, default=float) + ";\n")
print("ok", {k: v.get("tail") for k, v in runs.items()}, "kirman tv", round(tv, 4), "crash days", a, b)
PYEOF

  ## Motion research for the herding web app (Streamlit 1.67, Plotly 6.x/7.1 installed)
  
  **What I could load:** I fetched Linear, Robinhood Legend and Hyperliquid. The fetcher returns only page text, with no CSS or JS, so none of them gave durations or easing values. Hyperliquid has a repeated asset strip, which looks like a looping ticker, and "$ --" price placeholders, which look like skeleton states. Robinhood Legend promises "sub-second" updates and linked widgets. I did not fetch Coinbase Advanced, Kraken Pro, Public, Composer, Phantom, Vercel, Stripe or Raycast because of the time limit. So the patterns below are the common industry ones from my own knowledge, not measured from those sites. Treat the ms values as good defaults, not quotes.
  
  **Common patterns:**
  - **Price ticks:** a green or red background flash of about 150 ms in, then a 400–600 ms fade. Robinhood, Coinbase and Kraken use digit rolls (odometer), where each digit slides about 300–450 ms on ease-out.
  - **Charts:** the line draws in over about 600–900 ms when it first appears. Changing time range morphs the line in about 300 ms (Robinhood).
  - **Segmented controls:** a highlight pill slides about 200–250 ms with cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) (Linear, Vercel, Raycast).
  - **Cards:** on hover they lift 1–2 px and the border or glow brightens over 120–150 ms.
  - **Live dots:** a ring scales from 1 to 2.2 and fades out on a 1.5–2 s loop.
  - **Skeletons:** a shimmer sweeps across on a 1.2–1.6 s linear loop.
  - **Section entrance:** fades up 8 px over 200–300 ms, staggered 30–50 ms per item.
  - **⌘K palettes:** open over about 150 ms (scale .98 to 1 plus a fade).
  
  **Rerun facts that limit what works here:**
  - Streamlit re-mounts a changed element on every rerun, so CSS entrance animations replay. Animate only when a value changes.
  - A Streamlit element with the same `key` and position updates in place: the React wrapper calls `Plotly.react`. Two things here are unverified:
    - Plotly animates `layout.transition` only for some updates (mainly scatter/bar data on cartesian axes).
    - I found no documentation or forum evidence that it survives `st.plotly_chart`. Forums report the Plotly setting that keeps zoom across updates (`uirevision`) broke in Streamlit 1.10–1.13, and Plotly animation frames froze in 1.15–1.16.
    - **Test locally** before relying on chart morphs: one keyed chart, `fig.update_layout(transition={'duration':300,'easing':'cubic-in-out'})`, move a slider.
  - The app already injects CSS with `st.html(...)` and a script with `unsafe_allow_javascript=True` (`web/common.py` lines 354–355). It also already has a `blink` keyframe with a reduced-motion guard (lines 240–241).
  
  ## Ranked ideas
  
  1. **Value-change flash on metrics and the ticker tape.**
     - Keep the previous value in `session_state[f"prev_{k}"]`. Add class `up` or `dn` only if the value changed.
     - CSS: `@keyframes flash{0%{background:rgba(255,176,0,.28)}100%{background:transparent}}` with `.up,.dn{animation:flash 600ms cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) 1}`, and green or red text for `.up`/`.dn`.
     - Replay is safe because the class is absent when the value did not change.
     - Reduced motion: no animation, just the color.
  2. **Odometer digit roll** for the live header price, which refreshes every 15 s.
     - Each digit is a vertical strip of 0–9: `transform:translateY(-N em)` with `transition:transform 380ms cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)`.
     - It only animates if the DOM persists. With a re-mount, render from the old value and switch to the new one in a script inside `requestAnimationFrame`.
     - Only worth it for that one number. Reduced motion: swap the number instantly.
  3. **Live pulse dot** next to "LIVE" and the as-of time.
     - `::after{animation:ping 1.6s cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1) infinite}` with `@keyframes ping{75%,100%{transform:scale(2.2);opacity:0}}`.
     - A continuous loop, so a replay is invisible. Reduced motion: a static dot.
  4. **Hover lift on the bordered boxes.**
     - `transition:border-color 140ms ease, box-shadow 140ms ease, transform 140ms ease`, then `:hover{border-color:var(--amber);box-shadow:0 0 0 1px var(--amber),0 0 18px rgba(255,176,0,.15);transform:translateY(-1px)}`.
     - Hover is not tied to reruns, so there is no replay risk. Reduced motion: change color only, no transform.
  5. **Sliding highlight on segmented controls** (`st.segmented_control` / `st.radio` horizontal).
     - Pure CSS cannot slide between buttons that are re-mounted.
     - A fake version: `[aria-checked=true]{transition:background 180ms, color 180ms}`.
     - A real slide needs a script that measures the old and new button and animates a pill element using a FLIP animation (record the old position, then move to the new one) over 220 ms, cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1).
     - Medium effort and fragile, because Streamlit's DOM changes between versions.
  6. **Chart line draw-in, only on the first view of a page.**
     - The path sets `stroke-dasharray` to its length and animates `stroke-dashoffset` from the full length to 0 over 700 ms, ease-out.
     - Plotly redraws the SVG path on hover and relayout, so run it once from a script after `plotly_afterplot`. Guard it with a `sessionStorage` flag per chart so reruns do not replay it.
     - Reduced motion: skip it.
  7. **Native Plotly morph between herding-strength settings,** if the local test above passes.
     - Requires a stable `key`, the same trace count, and `transition` at 300 ms cubic-in-out.
     - If it fails, fall back to a 150 ms opacity crossfade on the chart container, only when the input changed.
  8. **Skeleton shimmer while heavy model runs compute.**
     - `st.empty()` shows a placeholder box: `background:linear-gradient(90deg,#111 0,#1d1d1d 50%,#111 100%);background-size:200% 100%;animation:shim 1.3s linear infinite`.
     - It is replaced when the result is ready. This beats Streamlit's own spinner and is safe on reruns.
  9. **Staggered section entrance, first visit only.**
     - Set `session_state.seen[page]=True` after the first render. Add the class `enter` only before that.
     - `@keyframes up{from{opacity:0;transform:translateY(8px)}}` at 240 ms ease-out, with an `animation-delay` of `calc(var(--i)*40ms)`.
     - Without the guard, every slider move makes the page "bounce", which is the main risk to avoid.
  10. **Keyboard shortcuts and a ⌘K palette.**
      - Single keys are feasible with one injected `keydown` listener on `window.parent.document`. Ignore keys when focus is in an input. Example keys: 1–6 jump to pages by clicking the `st.page_link`/nav anchors, `/` focuses the ticker search, `t` toggles the theme.
      - A real ⌘K palette is possible as a small overlay the injected script builds itself: a list of the pages and main controls that clicks the matching element.
        - It cannot call Python directly. It can only click or navigate, or set URL query params (`st.query_params`) that the app reads.
        - Moderate effort, and it breaks if Streamlit changes its DOM or iframe structure.
      - ⌘K itself conflicts with some browsers' search-bar shortcuts. Call `preventDefault`, and offer `Ctrl+K` as well.
  
  **General rules:**
  - One global guard: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce){*{animation:none!important;transition:none!important}}`.
  - Keep every animation at or under 600 ms, except the loops.
  - Never animate on a rerun without a "changed" or "first view" check.
  
  **Sources:**
  - [uirevision broken since Streamlit 1.10](https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/plotly-uirevision-parameter-no-longer-working-since-streamlit-version-1-10-0/28860)
  - [Plotly animation frozen in Streamlit 1.15–1.16 (issue #5881)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5881)
  - [Plotly.js animations](https://plotly.com/javascript/animations/)
  - [st.plotly_chart docs](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/charts/st.plotly_chart)
